reason: This is the only offered action, and collisions should advance the orbiting debris toward forming the Moon.
expectation: The collisions may change or gather the debris, though I’m unsure what form it will take.

effect: The collisions spread the debris into a ring, setting up a choice between its outward and inward paths.
reaction: The clarification that the ring is not solid is useful.
reason: I’ll follow the material beyond the tidal disruption region toward forming the Moon.
expectation: Some debris may be able to gather beyond the disruption region, though I’m unsure what intermediate form it takes.

alternatives.reason: Gravity may return debris to Earth, but I’ll pursue the Moon first.

effect: Beyond the disruptive tidal region, the debris can form surviving moonlets, so gravity is the next step toward a Moon.
reaction: The connection between tidal disruption and where clumps survive is useful.
reason: I’ll continue gathering the moonlets toward the Moon goal.
expectation: Gravity will bring the moonlets together into a larger body, perhaps the young Moon.

alternatives.reason: Returning debris to Earth also serves a goal, but I’ll finish the Moon path first.

effect: The moonlets have gathered into a hot young Moon; it still needs to cool for the crust goal.
reaction: Gathering the moonlets into a satellite feels like clear progress.
reason: I’ll cool the young Moon to pursue its crust.
expectation: The Moon should lose heat to space and begin forming a crust, though it may take another step.

alternatives.reason: Returning debris to Earth is also a goal, but I’ll finish the Moon path first.

effect: Cooling produced lunar magma-ocean crystals rather than a finished crust, so they are the next step toward it.
reaction: The distinction between sinking and floating minerals is useful.
reason: I’ll combine the crystals with the young Moon to continue forming its crust.
expectation: Some crystals may form a lunar crust, perhaps by floating, though I’m unsure whether that completes the goal.

alternatives.reason: Returning debris to Earth remains a goal, but I’ll finish the Moon path first.

effect: Buoyant plagioclase has formed a layer within the Moon; further cooling may complete the crust.
reaction: The explanation of why the crystals float makes the crust formation clearer.
reason: I’ll continue cooling the floating layer to finish the Moon path.
expectation: The layer will cool into a lunar crust, possibly completing the goal.

alternatives.reason: Returning debris to Earth remains necessary, but I’ll finish the crust first.

effect: The Moon’s early crust is complete, leaving the inward-falling debris goal.
reaction: The distinction between the pale early crust and later dark maria is interesting.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should advance the remaining goal.
expectation: Gravity will pull some ring material inward toward Earth, perhaps requiring another step to return it.

effect: The ring’s inward-moving rock is falling back toward Earth; combining it with the surviving planet should finish the remaining goal.
reaction: The split between Moon-forming and returning debris is clear.
reason: This is the only offered combination and directly pursues the remaining goal.
expectation: The falling rock will return to Earth, completing the debris-return goal.

effect: The falling debris returned to Earth, adding heat and material and completing the remaining goal.
reaction: The two paths for the impact debris came together clearly.

mostWorthwhile.text: Forming the floating feldspar-rich layer was most worthwhile: buoyancy explains how a lunar crust could develop from a magma ocean.

leastWorthwhile.text: The final return-to-Earth sequence felt least engaging because its two combinations were straightforward and each was the only offered action.

surprise.text: I was struck that debris could form surviving moonlets only outside the most disruptive tidal region.

arbitrary.text: Combining the crystals with the hot Moon felt somewhat abstract as an action, though the result explained that crust formation happens within the Moon.

continue.text: Yes. I would continue to see how the remade Earth cools and develops, especially after learning that some volatiles remain.
